programme.name: The Footballer's Week
programme.notes: Four gym sessions, one home mobility day, football at the weekend. Sessions capped at 70 minutes. Exercises marked phase1Excluded are deferred until the week-5 reassessment and must not appear in any day's blocks.

exercises.name: 90/90 rotation · Running pigeon · KB hip opener

progression.label: Fixed
progression.note: Warm-up. Progress range of motion over months, never load.

exercises.cue: Hips open before anything fast happens.

alternatives.name: World's greatest stretch
alternatives.reason: no space to sit on the floor

exercises.name: Banded lateral walk

progression.label: ↑ Band tension
progression.note: Progress by moving to a stiffer band, not by walking further.

exercises.cue: Stay low, no bobbing. Tension on the band the whole way.

exercises.name: Scapular rolls · Band rotator cuff · Dead bug

progression.label: Fixed
progression.note: Preparation. Nothing here should get harder.

progression.label: Fixed
progression.note: Maintenance.

exercises.name: Agility ladder

progression.label: Fixed
progression.note: A coordination warm-up, not agility training — real agility is unplanned. Do not progress it.

exercises.cue: Warm and unfatigued. Quick feet, tall posture.

alternatives.name: Line hops · fast feet on a step

progression.label: ↑ Range
progression.note: Progress range, not load. A desk day plus a bike commute shortens both of these.

exercises.name: Side-lying hip abduction

progression.label: ↑ Reps, then band
progression.note: Add reps to 20, then add a band. Hip strengthening has better evidence for anterior knee pain than anything done at the knee itself.

exercises.cue: Slow. No rocking backwards — the foot stays slightly behind the hip.

progression.label: ↑ Reps
progression.note: Bodyweight maintenance. The loaded version lives on Day 5.

exercises.name: Heavy sled push

progression.label: ↑ Load
progression.note: Your in-gym acceleration work, and the most knee-tolerant leg exercise available. Heavy enough that you're driving, not jogging.

exercises.cue: Low body angle, long drives, full extension each step.

alternatives.name: Steep incline treadmill walk, holding dumbbells

exercises.name: Trap bar jump

progression.label: ↑ Bar speed
progression.note: Around 20–30% of your trap bar deadlift and it stays there. Bar speed is the metric — when it slows, the set is over. Adding load turns this into a strength exercise and deletes the point of it.

exercises.cue: Land soft and shallow.

alternatives.name: Countermovement jump, bodyweight
alternatives.reason: knee sore, or no trap bar

alternatives.name: Extra sled push set
alternatives.reason: knee sore — swap the jump out entirely

exercises.name: Pogo jump · Banded pogo jump

progression.label: ↑ Ground contact
progression.note: Progress is shorter, stiffer ground contact — not height and not load.

exercises.cue: Stiff legs, almost no knee bend, quick off the floor. Nearly all ankle — which is why these survived the knee cut.

exercises.name: Skater jump, stick each landing

progression.label: ↑ Distance, quiet landings
progression.note: Progress distance and landing control. Never add load.

exercises.cue: Sideways, shallow, controlled. Hold each landing for a full second — the stick is the whole point.

progression.label: ↑ Speed, not ball weight
progression.note: A power exercise, not a conditioning one. Throw hard, rest fully, stop when speed drops.

progression.label: ↑ Distance
progression.note: Not in Phase 1 blocks — available as an alternative once the knee settles.

exercises.name: Trap bar deadlift

progression.label: ↑ 2.5–5 kg/wk
progression.note: The day's force-production lift. Hip-dominant and knee-friendly, which is why it survived the knee modifications intact. Heavy, but stop two reps short of failure.

exercises.cue: Push the floor away. Neutral spine, chest up, lock out tall.

exercises.name: Split squat to a box, flat-footed

progression.label: ↑ 2.5 kg/wk
progression.note: Knee-modified replacement for the heel-elevated version. Set the box where it's comfortable and lower it slightly each week as symptoms settle — depth is the first progression, load the second.

exercises.cue: Flat back foot, torso tall, sit straight down to the box. No heel elevation in Phase 1.

alternatives.name: Single-leg press, partial range
alternatives.reason: knee sore — machine supports the back

exercises.name: Hip thrust

progression.label: ↑ 2.5–5 kg/wk
progression.note: Serious posterior chain loading with the knee barely involved — which is exactly why it's in the Phase 1 plan.

exercises.cue: Pause a full second at the top. Ribs down, chin tucked.

exercises.name: Single-leg press, partial range

progression.label: ↑ 5 kg/wk
progression.note: Stop well short of deep. The machine supports your back, so this can be loaded hard without the depth that aggravates the knee.

exercises.cue: Foot high on the platform. Do not let the knee travel past comfortable.

exercises.name: DB step up, low box

progression.label: ↑ 2.5 kg/wk
progression.note: Knee-height or lower in Phase 1. Box height is a progression in its own right — raise it only after the knee settles.

exercises.cue: Step down slowly. The lowering is the part that builds control.

exercises.name: Single-leg RDL

progression.label: ↑ 2 kg/wk
progression.note: Trains the hip end of the hamstring. Nordics train the knee end. You need both.

exercises.cue: Hinge at the hip, flat back, slow on the way down.

exercises.name: Spanish squat isometric

progression.label: ↑ Time, then band
progression.note: The best-tolerated quad loading available when the front of the knee is sore, and it often reduces pain during the set itself — that's expected, not a fluke. Progress hold time to 60s, then move to a stiffer band.

exercises.cue: Heavy band behind the knees, anchored in front. Shins vertical, sit back, hold around 45°.

alternatives.name: Leg extension isometric hold, partial range

exercises.name: Wall sit at a comfortable angle

progression.label: ↑ Time, then depth
progression.note: Home version of the Spanish squat. Go only as deep as stays quiet — shallow is fine, holding is the point.

alternatives.name: Spanish squat isometric
alternatives.reason: at the gym with a band

exercises.name: Backward sled pull

progression.label: ↑ Load or distance
progression.note: Loads the quad hard with very little compression through the knee joint. The best knee exercise in the gym and the last thing to cut when short on time.

exercises.cue: Walk backwards, stay low, full knee extension each step.

progression.label: ↑ Load or distance
progression.note: Lighter and faster than the Day 1 heavy push — this one is about repeated drives, not maximal force.

exercises.name: Nordic hamstring curl

progression.label: ↑ Reps & range
progression.note: NEVER add weight. Bodyweight is already near the limit of what a hamstring can control eccentrically. Progress by lowering further under control and adding reps: 3×3 → 3×6 → 4×6. The best-evidenced hamstring injury reducer there is, and seriously sore for the first fortnight — which is why it sits six days from the match.

exercises.cue: Lower over four seconds. Hips straight, catch yourself with your hands.

exercises.name: Copenhagen plank

progression.label: ↑ Lever length
progression.note: The lever is the progression, not weight and not really time. Start knee-on-bench; after four sessions holding the top of the time range, move toward ankle-supported. Strong evidence behind it for groin injury prevention.

exercises.cue: Start on the short lever — knee on the bench. Hips high, body in one line.

exercises.name: Assisted pull-up

progression.label: ↓ Assistance 2.5 kg/wk
progression.note: The number on the machine goes DOWN each week, not up. Still progressive overload, just running backwards. Unassisted is the target.

exercises.cue: Full hang at the bottom, chest to the bar at the top.

progression.label: ↑ 2.5 kg/wk
progression.note: Your only horizontal press. Keep press volume at roughly half your pull volume across the week.

progression.label: ↑ 2.5 kg/wk
progression.note: Pull to the hip, not the chest. Let the shoulder blade travel.

exercises.name: Half-kneeling landmine press

progression.label: ↑ Add a plate
progression.note: Half-kneeling forces the trunk to brace — it's a core exercise wearing a press costume.

exercises.cue: Ribs down, glute of the back leg switched on, press across the body.

alternatives.name: Standing landmine press
alternatives.reason: kneeling is uncomfortable on the knee

progression.label: ↑ Reps, then load
progression.note: Small muscle, small jumps. Fill the rep range before adding anything.

progression.label: ↑ Reps, then load
progression.note: This plus your rows is what builds the shoulder-to-waist line, and what holds posture together at top speed.

exercises.name: Farmer's carry

progression.label: ↑ 2.5–5 kg/wk
progression.note: The cheapest proximal strength there is: trunk, scapulae and grip all braced under real load while walking.

exercises.cue: Heavy. Walk tall, don't lean.

alternatives.name: Suitcase carry, one side at a time

progression.label: ↑ Small increments
progression.note: Friday is a primer, not a test. Nothing to failure.

progression.label: ↑ 2 kg/wk
progression.note: Dumbbell increments are usually 2 kg per hand. Fill the range first.

progression.label: ↑ Reps, then load
progression.note: The incline puts the long head on stretch — that's the point of doing it seated back rather than standing.

progression.label: ↑ Reps, then load
progression.note: Overhead position loads the long head, which the pressing work doesn't reach.

progression.label: ↑ Small increments
progression.note: Anti-rotation. The goal is not moving, so load only as far as you can stay square.

progression.label: ↑ Slowly
progression.note: Striking a ball is a rotational act — everything your legs generate passes through here. Load this conservatively; speed of rotation matters more than weight.

progression.label: ↑ Slowly
progression.note: Rotation under an overhead load — trains the thoracic spine to turn while the hips stay stable.

progression.label: ↑ Slowly
progression.note: First to cut when short on time.

progression.label: ↑ Small increments
progression.note: The one piece of direct spinal flexion in the week. Everything else in the trunk work is anti-movement.

exercises.name: Calf raise

progression.label: ↑ 2.5–5 kg/wk
progression.note: Slow. Calves and Achilles absorb more running load than anything else you own, and they're the tissue that eats the most sprinting volume.

exercises.cue: Full stretch at the bottom, pause at the top.

progression.label: ↑ Reps
progression.note: Back against a wall, heels out, toes up. Builds shin tolerance for deceleration and landing.

exercises.name: Repeated-effort intervals — sled or ski erg

progression.label: ↑ Reps or shorter rest
progression.note: Sprint, recover badly, sprint again — the energy system football actually runs on. NOT the bike: the cycle commute already supplies that dose, and holding that dose steady is part of the knee plan.

progression.label: ↑ 2.5 kg/wk
progression.note: Deferred: heel elevation increases knee travel and therefore front-of-knee load. Reintroduce week 5 at low elevation, 2 sets, no added weight.

alternatives.name: Split squat to a box, flat-footed

progression.label: ↑ 2 kg/wk
progression.note: Deferred: slow eccentric knee flexion under load. Reintroduce week 5 from a low box.

progression.label: ↑ Height, slowly
progression.note: Deferred: landing is repeated high-force knee flexion. Reintroduce week 6 on a low box, 3×3. Always step down — never jump down.

progression.label: ↑ Height, slowly
progression.note: Deferred to week 6, after the double-leg version is tolerated.

progression.label: ↑ Ground contact
progression.note: Deferred to week 6. Trains the stretch reflex — the opposite quality to the seated box jump. Alternate the two once both are back.

progression.label: ↑ Height, slowly
progression.note: Deferred to week 6. Killing the stretch reflex trains pure starting strength.

progression.label: ↑ Distance
progression.note: Deferred to week 6. The broad jump landing is a hard deceleration.

progression.label: ↑ Range
progression.note: Deferred: a deep-range knee-health tool, which is the wrong range while symptomatic. Reintroduce week 7 at half the range you eventually want. Note this is a DIFFERENT exercise from a heavy hack squat — light load, deep range, tolerance-building.

progression.label: ↑ Quiet landings
progression.note: Deferred to week 8. Land quietly — noise is uncontrolled force. The training effect and the risk both sit in the landing.

progression.label: ↑ Range, then reps
progression.note: Deferred to week 9+: the highest front-of-knee load in the whole programme. Bodyweight, partial range, no rush.

progression.label: ↑ Range, then reps
progression.note: Deferred to week 9+. Deep, single-leg and unsupported — the last thing to come back.

progression.label: ↑ 2.5 kg/wk
progression.note: Deferred to week 9+: high kneecap load for what it returns while symptomatic.

prescription.note: Warm-up and knee work in one.
If the front of the knee complains, drop this and add a sled set.

prescriptions.note: Start at 3 reps. Never add weight.

days.title: Upper Strength + Trunk
days.note: Pull volume beats press volume, roughly 2:1. That ratio builds the back and holds posture together at speed.

days.title: Recovery + Mobility — at home
days.note: Genuinely easy, and not a gym trip. The cycle commute already covers the aerobic work. If it starts feeling like a session, it has gone too far.

prescription.note: Add clamshells here if you want the extra volume.
Add banded pogos for the last two sets if available.
Last thing to cut when short on time.

days.title: Upper, Rotation + Primer
days.note: Nothing to failure. This session keeps you sharp; it is not meant to be impressive. If you are playing twice this week, this is the session that goes.

reintroductionSchedule.startAt: Low elevation / low box, 2 sets, no added weight
Low box, 3 × 3. Step down, never jump down.
Half the range you eventually want
